sentences.text: She got it out of Madame Grandjean in the September, and she got it by doing the one thing thirty years of adults had not done, which was to ask a question about something else.
Madame Grandjean was ninety-three and had been eleven in 1944 and had lived in the last house before the ford her entire life.
Sidonie went down there on a Wednesday with a school project about the war that was real, that she had actually been set, and that she had chosen deliberately.
She did not ask about the toad.
She asked about the wood.
This was not cunning.

She had thought about it for a fortnight and arrived at it honestly: every adult in that village had spent sixty years declining one specific question, and it had not occurred to any of them, or to her grandfather, that the question was the wrong shape.
And Madame Grandjean, who had declined the other question from four generations of foresters, answered the one she was actually asked, and talked for an hour and ten minutes.
There had been people in that wood in the September of 1944.
Not soldiers — a family, and then two families, from Marche, in the four days when the front went through and nobody in that part of the Ardennes knew from one hour to the next whose road it was.
They were in the old sawmill, which was a ruin then as it is now, and there were nine of them and four were children.
The village fed them.
That is how Madame Grandjean, at eleven, was involved: she carried a basket down the track past the ford, in the evening, because a child with a basket is a child with a basket.
You went at dusk.

That was the arrangement and it was not negotiable — not in the light, because you would be seen, and not in the dark, because you could not find the sawmill in the dark and a torch was out of the question.

Madame Grandjean described the basket in detail — the cloth over it, the two jars, the weight of it on a child's arm at the point where the track goes up — and Sidonie understood that she had described that basket to herself a great many times over eighty years.
Dusk is about twenty minutes long and you had to be back over the ford before it closed.
"And on the third evening," said Madame Grandjean, "there was a patrol on the Bastogne road." Sidonie did not write anything down.
"I was on the track.

I heard them and I got into the ditch by the hornbeam and I lay there and I could not go on and I could not go back, and it was going dark, and my mother did not know where I was." She said that she had lain in that ditch for a long time.

She said that when she finally got up and went the rest of the way, it was still just light enough to find the sawmill, and that it should not have been, and that she had known it should not have been even at eleven, because she had walked that track at dusk every evening of her life.
"How long?" "About seven minutes," said Madame Grandjean.
